newsitem.title: INDIA: Israel's Weizman starts visit to India.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Weizman starts visit to India.

text.p: Israeli President Ezer Weizman said on Monday he felt terrific about his first visit to India, saying both countries shared a common legacy of British rule and their fight for independence from colonialism.

"My dear man, we did a bit of fighting ourselves with the British," Weizman said in response to an Indian reporter's question at the start of his official visit, a day after he arrived with a large business delegation.

Weizman was asked to compare his past as a British air force pilot in India in 1946 with his Indian host President Shankar Dayal Sharma, who campaigned non-violently against British rule at that time.
Weizman said: "You had the more difficult battle because you had them here for 200 years. We had them only for 30 years.
"Thank God both of us are independent now. You did it before us in 1947. It took us another year. But this is one common ground we have. The British and independence," he said.
"I feel terrific to be back here after 51 years," Weizman said after visiting the British-built Presidential Palace.
Indian diplomats last week said Weizman's visit would focus on the more than 100 joint ventures between Israel and India, most of them in agriculture.
His visit marks a high in relations that have strengthened since India established diplomatic ties with Israel in 1992 after decades of Cold War suspicions linked to the Palestinian problem.
India and Israel are expected to sign four agreements during Weizman's visit, including one on agriculture, officials said.

Indian companies have shown a keen interest in forming joint ventures with Israeli firms to make drip irrigation equipment. Indian officials say Israel's water-conservation technology could be of great use in India's dry zones.
Weizman's talks with Sharma and Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda would also include the current crisis in the Middle East over the West Bank town of Hebron.
"It's not an easy problem. It's a difficult solution. But I am sure (there would be progress) in the very near future, I don't want to quote dates," Weizman said.
He said he had spoken to Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai on Monday morning to discuss the issue.
Mordechai held a 90-minute meeting with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat in the self-ruled Gaza Strip on Sunday when they discussed the standoff over Hebron.

He said Israeli negotiators would settle the last disputes over Hebron so that by Monday evening Arafat and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu could set a time to sign the accord. The pact would give Palestinians control of 80 percent of the town.
